title: React for the Web and the Browser

questions.question: What are event bubbling and delegation?
options: The event travels from the document to the element, and delegation cancels it
The event rises from the element to its ancestors; delegation means one handler on a container instead of a handler on every element
Bubbling only works for mouse events
Delegation means passing a handler down through props
questions.explanation: The phases are capture → target → bubbling. Delegation saves memory and works for elements added dynamically. React for its part uses synthetic events and a single root listener (since React 17 on the render container rather than on document).
followUp: How does stopPropagation differ from preventDefault?

questions.question: What is the critical rendering path?
options: The order in which JS modules load inside the bundle
The path from receiving the HTML to the first painted frame: DOM → CSSOM → render tree → layout → paint
The route a request takes from the browser to the server
The priority of CSS rules when selectors conflict
questions.explanation: Blocking resources lengthen this path: a synchronous <script> in <head> stops HTML parsing, and CSS blocks rendering. Hence defer/async, inlined critical CSS, and preloading fonts.
followUp: What is the difference between defer and async?

questions.question: What do the Core Web Vitals — LCP, INP, CLS — measure?
options: Network speed, bundle size and request count
How long the main content takes to paint, how responsive interactions are, and visual stability
Test coverage, code complexity and error count
Time to first byte, DNS resolution and the TLS handshake
questions.explanation: LCP is when the largest element painted; INP (which replaced FID) is the delay in responding to interactions; CLS is how much the layout jumps. CLS is most often ruined by images without explicit dimensions and fonts without fallback metrics.
followUp: How do you connect these metrics to actual conversion?

questions.question: What is CORS?
options: A client-side protection mechanism against XSS
A mechanism by which the server allows the browser to read the response to a cross-origin request
An encryption protocol for cross-domain requests
A way to share cookies between subdomains
questions.explanation: The restriction is imposed by the browser, and the permission is granted by the server through Access-Control-Allow-* headers. The request usually goes out and executes — the browser simply refuses to let you read the response. "Complex" requests are preceded by a preflight OPTIONS. Important: CORS does not protect the server, it protects the user.
followUp: Why does CORS not save you from CSRF, and what does?

questions.question: How does a cookie differ from localStorage?
options: A cookie is sent to the server automatically with every request
A cookie has a lifetime and the HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite flags
localStorage is readable from JS, so it is vulnerable to theft through XSS
localStorage synchronises between tabs automatically
questions.explanation: For tokens a cookie with HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite is safer, because JS cannot reach it. localStorage is more convenient for non-secret data. There are storage events between tabs, but that is not automatic state synchronisation.
followUp: What does SameSite=Lax do and what does it protect against?

questions.question: What is hydration in React?
options: Fetching data after a component mounts
Attaching React to already-rendered server markup: wiring handlers and restoring state without repainting
Caching render output on the server
Loading images progressively as you scroll
questions.explanation: The server sends finished HTML — the user sees content quickly, but the page is not interactive yet. Hydration brings it to life. Hence the classic bug: if the server and client markup diverge (a date, Math.random, window), React complains about a mismatch.
followUp: What are streaming SSR and selective hydration?

questions.question: How do Server Components (RSC) differ from SSR?
options: They are the same thing under different names
SSR renders HTML on the server and hydrates it on the client; RSC never send their JS to the client at all
RSC only work together with GraphQL
SSR is only available in Next.js, while RSC work in any React app
questions.explanation: RSC execute on the server only: their code and dependencies never reach the bundle, and they can talk to a database directly. They have no state and no effects. Client components ('use client') work as usual. The main win is bundle size and data access without an API layer.
followUp: Why are RSC still barely applicable in React Native?

questions.question: How does a controlled component differ from an uncontrolled one?
options: A controlled one keeps the value in React state and updates through onChange; an uncontrolled one keeps the value in the DOM itself
Controlled only works with forms, uncontrolled with any element
An uncontrolled component cannot be validated
The only difference is having a defaultValue attribute
questions.explanation: Controlled gives full control and instant validation but re-renders the component on every character — noticeable in a large form. Uncontrolled (through a ref or defaultValue) is faster and simpler. Libraries like react-hook-form deliberately use uncontrolled inputs for performance.
followUp: Why do controlled inputs become a bottleneck in a large form?

questions.question: What are portals for?
options: Rendering a component into a different DOM node while keeping its place in the React tree
Passing data deep down without props
Loading components on demand
Isolating a component's styles
questions.explanation: Modals, tooltips and dropdowns suffer from a parent's overflow: hidden and z-index. A portal moves them to the end of body, but events still bubble up the React tree rather than the DOM — that is the key detail interviewers ask about.
followUp: How is the equivalent implemented in React Native?

questions.question: What is code splitting and how is it done in React?
options: Organising code into folders by feature
Breaking the bundle into parts loaded on demand — through a dynamic import() and React.lazy + Suspense
Extracting shared code into a separate monorepo package
Minifying and stripping unused code
questions.explanation: Usually the split follows routes: the user downloads only the screen they opened. React.lazy takes a function with a dynamic import, and Suspense shows a fallback while it loads. Stripping unused code is tree shaking, a different technique.
followUp: How does code splitting relate to inline requires in React Native?

questions.question: What is XSS and how do you defend against it?
options: Forging a request from another site; defended with CSRF tokens
Injecting someone else's script into the page; defended with output escaping, CSP, and care with dangerouslySetInnerHTML
Intercepting traffic; defended with HTTPS
Brute-forcing passwords; defended with rate limiting
questions.explanation: React escapes everything it inserts into markup by default, so basic XSS is rare in it. Holes appear where escaping is bypassed: dangerouslySetInnerHTML, href="javascript:", inserting a user-supplied URL into src. Forging a request from another site is CSRF, a separate attack.
followUp: What does a Content Security Policy do?

questions.question: How does Cache-Control: no-cache differ from no-store?
options: They are synonyms
no-cache allows storing but requires revalidation before use; no-store forbids storing at all
no-cache only applies to images
no-store caches the response in memory but not on disk
questions.explanation: The name no-cache is misleading: the response is stored, but before use it is validated through ETag or Last-Modified, and the server may answer 304. no-store is for genuinely sensitive data. For hashed static assets you use max-age of a year plus immutable.
followUp: How does caching work for static files with a hash in the name?

questions.question: What does HTTP/2 give you over HTTP/1.1?
options: Traffic encryption
Multiplexing requests over one connection, header compression, prioritisation
WebSocket support
Automatic response caching
questions.explanation: In HTTP/1.1 requests on a connection went one after another, hence head-of-line blocking and practices like sprites and bundle concatenation. HTTP/2 sends them in parallel over one connection, so splitting a bundle into many files became normal. Encryption comes from TLS, not from the protocol version.
followUp: Which HTTP/2 problem does QUIC solve in HTTP/3?

questions.question: What is a Service Worker?
options: A background thread for heavy computation
A proxy between the app and the network: it intercepts requests and enables offline mode and background sync
A server-side process that serves SSR
A mechanism for isolating a component's styles
questions.explanation: This is what PWAs are built on. It only works over HTTPS, has its own lifecycle (install → activate) and its own headache around updates: an old worker can keep serving a cached version. Heavy computation is a Web Worker, a different thing.
followUp: How does a Web Worker differ from a Service Worker?

questions.question: What is CSS specificity and how is it calculated?
options: Declaration order: the last rule always wins
Selector weight: inline > id > class/attribute/pseudo-class > tag; on a tie the last one wins
The number of characters in the selector
How deeply the element is nested in the DOM
questions.explanation: !important beats everything except another !important of higher specificity — and it is a sign that the style architecture has gone off the rails. Modern approaches (CSS modules, CSS-in-JS, utility classes) exist largely so you do not have to fight specificity.
followUp: How do CSS modules solve this, and why does the problem not exist in RN at all?

questions.question: What is accessibility (a11y) and what do you check first?
options: Load speed for users on a slow connection
Semantic markup, keyboard navigation, contrast, alt text and labels, correct ARIA roles
Responsive layout across screen sizes
Support for old browsers
questions.explanation: The basic rule: a native semantic element beats a div with an ARIA role. The practical minimum is to walk the page using only Tab and check contrast. React Native has a direct equivalent: accessibilityLabel, accessibilityRole and working with the screen reader.
followUp: How is this tested automatically, and why do automated tests not catch everything?

questions.question: A page takes a long time to open. How will you find the cause? Answer out loud.
questions.explanation:
What is expected is a breakdown into stages, not a list of tips:

1. Network or client? Look at TTFB — if it is high, the problem is the backend or the network, not React
2. The waterfall in DevTools: what blocks, which resources are critical, are there needless round trips
3. Bundle size and composition: an analyser, heavy dependencies, missing code splitting
4. Rendering: the Performance tab, long tasks, too much work on the main thread
5. Images and fonts — a frequent cause of poor LCP and CLS
6. Measure before and after on a throttled network and a slow CPU

A strong answer specifically notes that you must measure under real user conditions, not on a fast laptop with a local server.
followUp: Which of these applies equally to a mobile app?
